entities.name: Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Assumption, Santiago de Cuba
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Assumption of Santiago de Cuba (Catedral Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción de Santiago de Cuba), founded in 1514 as one of the first Catholic cathedrals in the Americas following the Spanish colonization of Cuba, is the mother church of the Archdiocese of Santiago de Cuba and one of the oldest continuously functioning cathedrals in the Western Hemisphere — located in Cuba's second city and historic eastern capital, and serving as the religious center of a city that has been pivotal in Cuban history from the colonial period through the wars of independence and the Cuban Revolution.

Santiago de Cuba was established by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in 1515 as one of the original seven Spanish colonial settlements (villas) in Cuba, and was Cuba's first capital before Havana assumed that role. The Cathedral of the Assumption, built on the Plaza de Armas (now Parque Céspedes) facing the city hall, occupies the same symbolic space as the political authority — the characteristic colonial urban plan of church and state facing each other across the main plaza.

The cathedral's construction history spans five centuries: repeatedly rebuilt and renovated due to earthquakes and deterioration, the current primarily Baroque structure dates largely to the 17th-19th centuries. The tomb of Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, Cuba's first governor, was reportedly associated with the early cathedral. Santiago de Cuba's Afro-Cuban religious culture — where Santería, the syncretic Yoruba-Catholic religion, has been particularly strong — has created a complex religious landscape in which the cathedral's official Catholic presence coexists with a rich underground of African-derived religious practice.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Cathedral Basilica of Santiago de Cuba — one of the Western Hemisphere's oldest cathedrals (1514), mother church of the first Cuban capital, and religious center of a city crucial to Cuban history from colonialism through Revolution — is an important monument of Spanish American religious and colonial history.
